utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we call the witness, the Trial Chamber has some rulings to make. The first one is concerning the witness Simo Jovanovic, who had a Rule 92 statement. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the evidence on record for all three accused persons, and especially the evidence regarding persons trained in Ilok. The Trial Chamber has decided to revise its ruling concerning Simo Jovanovic because it finds that it's no longer necessary to hear him orally as his statement has covered the relevant aspects of the evidence touching the charges against the accused. So he will come for cross-examination, and thereafter be re-examined, as ruled previously. The second ruling is concerning the motion, the oral motion by the Defence to submit the expert opinion of General Richard W. Wilmot, rendered in the -- tendered in the Stakic case. The Trial Chamber has noted that the Prosecution filed their response out of time. It was supposed to be filed on the 22nd of April. But has considered it in the interests of justice and has decided to allow the Defence motion to have the expert opinion report submitted in this case. The Trial Chamber has also decided to admit the transcript of the testimony of General Wilmot recorded in the Stakic case, so that all the relevant matters will be on record for consideration by the Trial Chamber. On Friday, we shall be sitting in the morning as of tomorrow. Today we allowed the afternoon session to allow the counsel who were travelling to travel this morning. On Friday, at 0900 hours, the Trial Chamber would like to hear submissions from the Defence and the Prosecution regarding the exhibits touching on the agreements of the International Red Cross. This is Exhibit D190/3, D192/3, and D193/3, submitted by the Defence. We just want to know, briefly, what the relevance of these agreements are to the defence of the accused. We would also like to know, briefly, in the same vein, on the Prosecution agreements also Exhibit P176, 177, 178, and 179. We would also like to hear the Prosecution briefly as to the relevance of these agreements, or otherwise to the case of the Prosecution. We shall now proceed and call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought in, there are several documents. I notified Chamber's legal officer of this today. While reviewing the Prosecution's search material last week in relation to this witness Mr. Mitrovic, the Prosecution found six documents, Crisis Staff documents, bearing the signature of Mitar Mitrovic, which we have had translated and served on the Defence Thursday by fax last week. That was the B/C/S version. The translated versions are here. The Prosecution would intend -- they're not particularly controversial documents at all. They just relate to matters which he appeared to be involved in in the running of the affairs in Bosanski Samac in the relevant period. The Prosecution would intend to put these documents to Mr. Mitrovic in the course of its cross-examination. We note that Your Honours provided, through the Chamber's legal officer, on Wednesday a list of some 34 exhibits which the Trial Chamber wishes to use in its examination of Mr. Mitrovic. The Prosecution is wondering if it would be appropriate for the Prosecution to tender these six documents or show them to the Trial Chamber first to see whether they would assist the Trial Chamber in its examination of Mr. Mitrovic. The documents just range from an authorisation to secure all necessary assistance in the country and abroad on behalf of the municipality, to authorisation to systematically collect boat motors for the VRS, signed by the Crisis Staff, lending Mr. Vaso Antic a video camera for use in filming war operations in Posavina, adding two workers to the War Presidency payroll, that's Biljana Raulic and Ana Mitrovic, and the record on the keeping and using of the Crisis Staff stamps. The two stamps of the Bosanski Samac -- sorry the Samac Crisis Staff, 14 September 1992. Those are the sixth documents. I'm in Your Honours' hands as to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long has the Prosecution has had these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The documents, I think, were submitted by Mr. Mirko Lukic through Mr. Pisarevic [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "Pisarevic"] I think in 1998, I think. They only came to attention last week and the reason is this, because they actually had Mr. Mitar Mitrovic's name on them. The search of the system was specifically designed to pick up documents with Mr. Mitar Mitrovic's name on them and that's why the Trial Chamber only discovered them during course of last week. If they had been absolutely vital documents, I'm sure they would have been discovered in the Prosecution case a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. On the same matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours will allow me, on the same matter, on the same motion of the Prosecution, I would like to put forward the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say a few words, but I don't think it is the time for me to repeat myself. We have already gone over the same ground several times. A few months ago, or a month ago, the Prosecution appeared with a similar document during the cross-examination of one of the witnesses of the Defence, and then the documents were submitted. But this is something that happens very often. I have a very high professional opinion of my learned friends, but I cannot accept, if there is something that they have in their hands, and if there is an obligation for the documents to be disclosed to my colleagues, and if this is not disclosed until two or five days before the witness actually arrives. We have pointed this out several times when we had Witness Dragovic. The Rules before this Tribunal say that the Prosecution and the Defence are required to disclose documents immediately, those documents which may be of some relevance for the other side. It is indisputable with regard to what the Prosecution has just said, it is indisputable that these documents have been in their possession since 1997 and we only received them on Thursday, when they were faxed to us. We didn't see them before. What is very worrying and what is very important with regard to the decision that has already been made by the Trial Chamber with regard to two witnesses who testified here, who were members of the Crisis Staff. Now, after my witness has testified, we have received documents relevant and with regard to the Crisis Staff. There is no way for me to dispute these documents. The only thing I can do is to put questions about this document to this witness. My case with regard to this witness is over and there's no way I can do anything, and I cannot agree with the Prosecution using these documents at this moment. I believe that it is indisputable and that the Trial Chamber should apply the Rule from Article 89, when the Defence case is already over, this should have a higher force and priority over any document that is being introduced now, and the Defence has been deprived of any possibility to dispute these documents by any other legal means. I could ask the witness about -- questions about these documents, but what is disputable is whether the Defence can offer anything with regard to these seven or eight documents that could dispute these documents. From the very beginning of this trial, the Prosecution has been aware of that and as regards the defence of Miroslav Tadic, all the documents and all the exhibits that have been introduced have been provided to the Prosecution in due time. The only thing that was disclosed late was the minutes regarding Mr. Lukac, so the Prosecution, if they want to introduce these documents, they have to make us aware, they have to let us know why are they doing it only now, five years later. They are putting the Defence in a very -- in a bad position by doing that. I mentioned Mr. Lukac. I would like to correct myself, and I would like to say that this is the only time that the Defence introduce a new document which was only seven days old. Because during the testimony of Mr. Marko Kuresevic, when the Prosecution, in their examination, have come across the decisions of the Crisis Staff, the Trial Chamber was of the position, because the two defence cases were already over, that it wouldn't be fair for these documents to be presented, and they didn't allow the Prosecution to cross-examine Mr. Marko Kuresevic on the basis of these documents. I would like to point out that it is very important that this introduction and this kind of tendering of the documents is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I very briefly respond to that? There seems to be some misunderstanding here. Firstly, these documents were never part of the Prosecution case. There was no obligation to disclose them to the Defence during the Prosecution case. The Prosecution wasn't relying upon them. The Trial Chamber has decided to call Mitar Mitrovic, who was originally on Dr. Simic's list. As a result of that, the Prosecutor searched through its collection for any documents specific to this particular witness. It's as a result of that that these witnesses -- or these documents have come to light. So there's been no failure of a disclosure obligation, because the Prosecution basically had none in relation to these documents. We never intended to use them as part of our case. Secondly, none of these documents directly impact upon Mr. Tadic at all. They're just normal documents in the day-to-day running of the municipality. Documents we would put to a witness who is called in the course of his evidence. And we disclosed them when we found them, as soon as we found them. So there's been no breach of our obligation, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Re, there seems to be something missing on the transcript which might be relevant. If you could look to page 3, line 23, you had said the documents I think were submitted by Mr. Mirko Lukic through Mr., and we have a gap. I think in 1998, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Pisarevic is what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you said that too, but it's missing right now. So that is Mr. Borislav Pisarevic, counsel for Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's my understanding. I have to check on that, but all the documents which came through Mr. Lukic came through Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record as a matter of principle, I have to object to the submission and motion of my learned friend from Prosecution on the following basis: Assuming that Mr. Mitrovic, since he was on the previous list on Dr. Simic defence witness list, the question here is: The Prosecution was informed about the possible appearance of Mr. Mitrovic on our list. So the same situation could arise when he was here, if it was arranged, and then the obligation of Prosecution was established. So my learned friend cannot claim that it was a surprise for him that Mr. Mitrovic will come. He is informed of possible appearance of Mr. Mitrovic well in advance. So the question is: Why they did not disclose these documents at that stage? My objection is on the basis of principle, actually. Allowing this approach of my learned friend from Prosecution will open, will enter an area of legal insecurity, because in that case, everything -- every document could be introduced after the -- as a result of research engines and machines, et cetera, et cetera. We know very well that the permanent obligation of the Prosecution related to Rule 68, I believe, is permanent. But on the other aspect of procedural issues here, it's not allowed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say the following: I would like to support my colleagues, but I would also like to draw your attention to the following fact. When Mr. Re says that I was the one who delivered these documents, this is not correct. I saw them for the first time when I arrived here this morning. It is very possible that there was power of attorney who appeared in the defence of Mr. Simic. His name was Spasoje Pisarevic. It is possible that he delivered these documents. I never saw these documents before. So just for the transcript, I would like to correct that in the transcript, it was not me who did that. And as far as this situation is concerned, recently we've had Witness Vaso Antic, and one document of those which are tendered, which are tendered to be admitted through Mr. Mitrovic is also a document that is -- that concerned Mr. Vaso Antic. I believe that it would be fair, it would have been fair, for the Prosecution to have disclosed this document before Mr. Antic appeared as a witness here. Then we would have been in the position to cross-examine Mr. Antic about the circumstances described in this document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has considered the motion by the -- the oral motion by the Prosecution regarding the documents which they intend to produce and has also considered the submissions by the Defence. The Trial Chamber finds nothing convincing on the part of the Prosecution as to why these documents were not disclosed earlier, because the point is, it's not a question of any witness being called to give evidence. It's a question of what evidence the Prosecution requires to support their case. So the motion is denied. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have your full name on record, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mitar Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: 27th of May, 1964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What are your qualifications?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am a lawyer. I have a B.A. in law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is your current residence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Currently I reside in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In October 1991 -- between October 1991 and December 1993, where were you residing?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was residing in Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When did you move to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Samac -- I can't remember the exact date. Was it 1994, the beginning of 1994? I'm not sure. But I think that's when I moved to Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has evidence that you were appointed to work on the Crisis Staff sometime in 1992. The Trial Chamber would like to find out when exactly you were appointed, to serve on the Crisis Staff of the Bosanski municipality.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was not nominated or appointed as a member of the Samac municipality Crisis Staff. First of all, I should explain. This will take a longer explanation, I'm afraid, than merely one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: When war operations began in Samac, if I may actually call them that, I came, I think, on the 18th of April, 1992. I had been called in by the secretariat for National Defence of Samac municipality. In fact, representatives of the secretariat came for me and told me to report immediately to Samac, as someone who had been appointed the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Samac. As on the 15th of April, the state of imminent danger of war had been proclaimed in the territory of the then Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was given a war assignment, an obligation, by the secretariat, as an appointee for the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and I was told to report to Samac immediately. I arrived in Samac and went to a building. I think it was a company. I'm not sure what the company was actually doing. I think it was something about agriculture. When I arrived, I found a group of persons there. I was told, and I had seen that with my own eyes, that combat operations were being conducted at the bridge in Samac by the Sava River. I was also told that the organs, that the municipal organs, were not functioning properly and that I should carry out my duty until further notice, or rather, perform my duty until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Who told you to carry out your duties until further notice?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The secretary for National Defence of the municipality. I think his last name was Bogdanovic. And this was written down in my military record book, the one that I had to keep on me all the time. This was written down in it. My war assignment within the organs of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what exactly were your duties from then onwards?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As secretary of the Municipal Assembly, I performed this duty, until 1997. The duties and authorities of the secretary of the Municipal Assembly were regulated by the law and statute of the municipality. According to the regulations then in force and pursuant to the regulations in force now, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly has the following duty, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The Trial Chamber is not interested in the current situation. The Trial Chamber is interested in the situation during and 1993, what were your duties then. You said that this was your war assignment, so we're interested in what your duties were. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When I arrived in Samac, at that building - that was not the building of the Municipal Assembly - there were several people there. As I am not a native of Samac, there were quite many people I didn't know there, but I did know Mr. Blagoje Simic. I did know Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, Mr. Milan Simic, and some other people too. Well, can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What transpired?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was told on that occasion, Mr. Blagoje Simic told me, among other people there, that in view of the situation, the Municipal Assembly could not be convened, due to war operations. One would try to organise at least the minimum functioning of the municipal authorities, until conditions are created for the Municipal Assembly to be reconvened. Furthermore, there were -- I'm not sure if all of them exactly, but members of the Executive Board were there too. The Executive Board also had duties regulated by regulations and laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We just -- the Trial Chamber just wants to know about yourself and your duties. So you were informed by Blagoje Simic. How long did you perform these duties?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I'm not sure if on the same day or the next day, I was informed, the same place, the same building, that provisional, temporary Crisis Staff would need to be organised, or rather, established, as an ad hoc body to function on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Dr. Blagoje. And those people who were there, Milan Simic was there, I think, Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What's the first name of Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what transpired on the following days after that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Over the following that days, because the operations in Samac and in the surroundings of Samac did go on for a couple of days, we were in that building. Then we moved to the municipality building. And over those several days, we moved a number of times, because of armed operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you keep saying "we moved." Whom do you mean? Yourself and the members you found at the beginning, or were other people also attending?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those people who then, and in the meantime, some other people came along the joined the group. Dr. Blagoje said that a Crisis Staff should function and that this was going to continue for -- to last for a certain brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So now this -- the Crisis Staff was established. So what exactly were your functions in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I had already been appointed as secretary of the Municipal Assembly, my duty was to be there alongside with those people and to assist with the typing of certain documents which had been drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Who was drafting the documents?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was mostly typing these documents, and the acts, the documents, from the very beginning of the functioning of the Crisis Staff until the very end, were mostly proposed by the Executive Board or by members of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was this done during the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must explain this in the following way: For the first three months - May, June, and July - I was mostly staying in the village of Obudovac. I am a native of Obudovac and I resided there. I would go to Samac as necessary, and if called in, in order to type certain documents. Therefore, from the very beginning, there were people there from the Executive Board too, who, to a greater or lesser extent, made proposals for certain decisions to be passed and documents to be drafted. What actually happened? This Crisis Staff organises an ad hoc body. I'm telling you this as a lawyer. I'm telling you this as a witness to certain events from the period. The Crisis Staff, to a certain degree, in terms of its authority, stood in for the Municipal Assembly of Samac, replaced the Municipal Assembly. On the other hand, the Executive Board was fully appointed, or rather, elected, so it functioned -- it kept on functioning from the very beginning, to the best of my knowledge. The composition of the Crisis Staff, well, I must say that even now I can't think of all the members exactly with any degree of certainty, but I do know that certain people, also from the Executive Board, as an executive body, as an operative body, attended meetings, or rather, sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Besides the Executive Board, what other institution attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The few meetings at the beginning, May, late April and May 1992, were attended also by representatives of certain institutions, institutions of vital importance for the proper functioning of the town of Samac. Some had been appointed. Some came for what they were. I know that I do remember that some had even been appointed, because I myself typed those decisions on the typewriter, the decisions on their appointments. I remember some persons who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We want the names of these people and the institution they represented.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I typed up decisions for the following appointments for the directors, or rather, managers of certain crucial, essential institutions: The health centre of Samac, I believe it was Dr. Nogic, if memory serves me, Dr. Mesud Nogic, because I had typed that particular decision, and I remember that Dr. Mesud Nogic came personally to receive this decision from Dr. Simic. Then there was, I believe, the manager or director of a company, Utva or Uniglas. His last name was Zaimbegovic. He also came and received the decision on his appointment. Then the post office, the communications office, the water supply system, I believe, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So would you say that all the heads of institutions which provided essential services or which were considered important in the running of the municipality of Samac area were members of the Crisis Staff or were appointed to the membership of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: These people that I have just mentioned a little while ago as having been appointed, I believe that they only received decisions, but they were not members of the Crisis Staff. I was talking about some companies and institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I'm asking is: These heads of these institutions, were they attending meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that at some of the sessions that I attended in that building, or rather, in the offices occupied by the Crisis Staff, where the Crisis Staff held its meetings, that these people also came there. I assume that they came to deal with some issues relative to the functioning of those institutions, given the conditions that were in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Was it the case that -- then that each head of an institution would attend the meeting of the Crisis Staff, report on the activities of the institution, and then the Crisis Staff or the members would discuss that and take decisions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be appropriate to draw that as a general conclusion, because I did not attend all the sessions or meetings of the Crisis Staff. The fact is that these people did come, and probably they came to deal with the problems they experienced in their respective institutions at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but of the sessions that you attended, wasn't that the procedure, that they would discuss the problems in their institutions and then the Crisis Staff collectively would make a decision as to what should be done?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: At the few sessions that I attended, there were discussions about certain issues in the presence of those people, so they were there when problems were discussed. I believe that not only people from institutions came. There were also people from local communes, the Red Cross, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since you are saying that you weren't attending all the sessions of the meetings of the Crisis Staff, was there somebody else who was performing similar functions to yours on the days when you were not attending the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: When I was there, my task was to type the enactment, or the decision, which was passed at that particular meeting of the Crisis Staff. When I wasn't there, I really don't know how many sessions there were all together and what was discussed at all those sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are not asking about the sessions which you didn't attend. I'm asking you about the sessions which you attended. And let's stick to that, okay. Was there a voting procedure? Were decisions carried by a majority or was there a quorum for decisions of the Crisis Staff to be passed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that there was no particular procedure in place. I assume that this was the case, because there were no conditions for the proper procedure to exist like it can in the peacetime. The voting that took place only took place at a few sessions, but you wouldn't call that a procedure like you would call it in peaceful situations, in normal situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Whoever attended that particular session, they would discuss and come to a decision and then you would type the decisions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of all the decisions that you typed, who would sign on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: These decisions were signed by Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Were there any decisions of the Crisis Staff which were typed by yourself and signed by yourself at any time at all?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what decisions those were, but there were cases when I typed a decision and I forwarded it to somebody and I had to sign it, to certify it, by my signature, before I forwarded it to somebody else, because I had -- in certain cases I was authorised by Dr. Simic to forward certain documents, certain enactments to other people, as a typed version of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Did such documents on which you were authorised by Dr. Simic carry your own signature or his signature?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember how many such documents there were. It is possible that there were such documents, but I'm sure I did it based on the authority given to me by Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The evidence before the Trial Chamber is that the Crisis Staff functioned up to about July, or thereabouts, then it changed its title to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long did the War Presidency function?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: For the first three months that I mostly spent outside of the seat of the Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff functioned, as far as I remember, in that particular form. I also remember that an enactment was published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. By that enactment, it was decided that in some municipalities in which there were no conditions in place for the functioning of the Municipal Assembly, as a body, that War Presidencies should be established in such municipalities. The Crisis Staff was, pursuant to that decision, renamed into War Presidency. I personally typed that decision, pursuant to the order that I received from Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Essentially, would you say that the membership remained the same?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, I was not told that the composition of the Crisis Staff would be changed and that some persons would no longer be members of this body and some new persons would become its members. So I can't tell you whether there were any officially appointed new members of the Crisis Staff or whether the old members of the Crisis Staff continued serving as members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But you did attend sessions of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As of the end of July, or maybe early August 1992, I attended several sessions of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For how long did the War Presidency function?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The War Presidency functioned, I believe, up to December 1992. I don't remember the date. The War Presidency, I believe, passed a decision, or maybe it was Dr. Blagoje Simic - I can't remember this for a fact - for the Municipal Assembly to be reconvened. In any case, the Executive Board was also involved in that, because the volume of the duties and tasks that the legislative body would have increased, so that the first session of the Municipal Assembly was convened in December. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: 1992. And I believe that the War Presidency functioned up to the next session of the Municipal Assembly, which took place either in January or in February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And throughout this period, Dr. Blagoje Simic was the president?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Were members of the Crisis Staff and later War Presidency paid a salary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: All the duties that had to do with salaries, all the executive duties, finances, were under the authority of the Executive Board, which probably in keeping with the conditions that were in place at that time, organised these things. Therefore, I wouldn't be able to tell you whether there are any records on the salaries of the members of the Crisis Staff exist as a separate set of document, separate from the documents about the salaries of the Executive Board. Those are municipal organs, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Were you yourself paid a salary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I received a salary, but I don't know when this started, when I started being paid. In any case, all the employees of the municipal organs did receive their salaries. I don't know when this started. I don't remember the date when we started being paid salaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When the War Presidency ceased to exist, did you continue your duties with the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Assembly ratified the decisions of the War Presidency, and I could then work as secretary of the Municipal Assembly, as a full-time employee, and that means that I assisted the president of the Municipal Assembly with the preparation of sessions, and I also performed other technical duties and tasks. The Executive Board could, after that, have better conditions to create a better procedure for proposing various decisions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Did you remain with the Municipal Assembly throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Judges will continue asking you further questions, especially regarding some of the decisions of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Mitrovic. We only have a couple of minutes before our break, or so. Let me just begin, before asking you some of the questions on various documents, just based on some of your answers to the Presiding Judge, Judge Mumba, I'm just wondering: You say you were not a native of Samac; you were from Obudovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. And you had your B.A., your law degree, and you were born in 1964, which would mean, if I'm correct in my arithmetic, you were about age 27 at the time you were appointed as secretary to the Crisis Staff. You've told us that all you did was to type documents, and I'm just wondering, as a matter of interest, interest to what is before us, what was somebody brought in from Obudovac with a law degree simply to type documents? Could you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I was appointed the secretary of the Municipal Assembly on the 28th of March. That's why I was called. This was simply my duty, my task. And if you were talking about proposals for various decisions, then I can tell you that this was neither my duty nor my authority. It was not within my purview, and that is simply something I couldn't do. I couldn't propose any decisions. In the Executive Board there were more experienced lawyers who participated in the drafting of those decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. And also referring to one of your answers to our Presiding Judge, you mentioned, and for the sake of counsel, this was page 14, lines 6 to 9, you mentioned that decisions and so on were proposed by the Executive Board or members of the Executive Board. But I don't think we got a clear response as to who actually drafted the wording of these decisions, conclusions, whatever the title of the particular document was. Who actually listened to the proposals and wrote them down and so on? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can certainly tell you, and I will repeat once again. I will tell you very openly. I was not the one who was creating the decisions and the enactments. During the sessions of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, sessions that I attended, there were always the representatives of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I understand that. But if you could just, you know, give me sort of a simple answer, if you could. There's a discussion, proposals are put on the table, so to speak. Somebody has to take those verbal proposals and put them onto paper. And I'd like to know who -- it could be several people at different times, but who did that. That would be the first question. And secondly, was then a draft circulated to all of the people who had been present to make sure that what was on paper reflected the sense of the discussion and the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. This is how it had to be done. I was not the one who was to decide anything, and I was not the one handing the document to Dr. Blagoje Simic for his signature. It could not have been that way. So therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You're not really answering my question. My question is: There's a discussion, a proposal is put on the table by one of the persons present. There's a discussion, somebody puts that now into written form. Is that you? Is that somebody else? Could you just answer me directly, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All the decisions and enactments were typed by myself on the typewriter. Those enactments that I typed on the typewriter, thanks to -- or through the notes. I used my notes to type them. Or I was making notes following the oral debate that took place during the sessions by members of the War Presidency. I was then hand them the notes. Then they would look at the notes. They would correct, if they wanted to correct something. And if something had to be changed, it was changed. And then it was finally put in a written form and then it was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now I'll just move on to some other questions that I'd be interested in hearing your response to. I wonder whether you know, and if you don't know, please just say you don't know: Did the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac declare itself the municipal government of Bosanski Samac on the orders of the SDS party at the national level? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The answer to this question cannot be given to you precisely. I do not have the details to answer correctly. I do not know if Dr. Blagoje Simic received all the orders stemming from the SDS in order to create the Crisis Staff. I do not have those details at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's just fine, and that -- if you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: But however, I know that Dr. Blagoje told me, when the Official Gazette of the municipality of Samac was created, he then told me that it's important to clarify and to put in writing that the SDS, or rather, its bodies, have created the municipality of Samac. That was the gist of what he told me. That is true. This is what I put down in writing. I changed it and I wrote it down. But it is a fact that the members, deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Samac were all appointed in 1990, during the local elections, and I believe that those were members of the SDS, aside from one person, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. What, in your view, based on your personal knowledge, was the actual role of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac? And I'll just mention two things that I have in mind that I'd like to have your view on, based on your personal knowledge. First of all, did the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac have to act in accordance with policies and positions of the national SDS party? Maybe I'll stop there and let you deal with that one first.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: To answer, I have to tell you that the SDS got the majority of votes during the elections of 1990. Of all the Serb electors, all the deputies belonged to the SDS. The Crisis Staff, if you want me to talk to you about its role, I think from a legal perspective maybe some jurists could give you a broader explanation of the concept of the Crisis Staff. I must tell you that up until then, I never encountered such body. But the situation was such that it was slightly strange. I, however, know, and I can tell you, that in 1992 political parties were forbidden to function at the level of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for a certain period of time. I cannot recall the exact time frame, but I can tell you that it was -- the work of these political bodies was forbidden. I do not know if all the members of the Crisis Staff were also members of the SDS. The deputies of the municipalities, yes, almost all of them were members, but in terms of the Crisis Staff, I couldn't tell you with more precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again, I'm wondering whether you know personally whether the -- before the setting up of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac, I'm wondering whether you have any knowledge as to whether the SDS party in Bosanski Samac received any message from Radovan Karadzic ordering a state of emergency situation for all SDS bodies, members, or officials. Are you aware of any such message?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Regarding such a message coming from Radovan Karadzic, or anybody from the top, who was at the top of the then SDS or Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I do not know if such a thing existed. I was not a member of the SDS. I was not involved in politics. But I know that on the 15th of April, 1992, a war -- imminent threat of war was proclaimed on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, I wonder whether you could take a look at a document. It's P3 ID. If the registry assistant could put the B/C/S version in front of you. This is the document entitled in the short form "variant A and variant B." Mr. Mitrovic, have you had a chance to look at this before this moment in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness answers, Your Honour said P3 ID. Our records show that it is actually in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And we're looking for the other ones. There were other ones that were admitted. My case manager is looking for it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In that case, it's P3. It's my mistake if I said ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an official list that it's ID. It was discussed with Dr. Robert Donia, 11th of September, 2001. It's ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Pantelic, I've been informed, P3 is admitted. P3A is the one that's the -- the piece out of the magazine that Dr. Donia referred to that he got from the archives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But the document that I'm looking at is actually the one which is copy number 100. So it's my mistake in mentioning ID. So, Mr. Mitrovic, you've had a chance to look at this particular document before this moment in time, right now in the court?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: First time. No. This is the first time I see this document, this text, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just have one question, which you've now answered, which was going to be: Are you familiar with the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I just read the first page in one part, second page, where I can see there is talk about the creation of the Crisis Staff and who would be its commander, so on and so forth. Yes, I can see that it's written here variant A, variant B. I can see that there is mention of the creation of the Crisis Staff. But to answer your question, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So you haven't seen it before. Have you -- did you ever hear, in 1992, while you were in your position as secretary to the Crisis Staff and so on, did you ever hear about variant A and variant B from any other person?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I've got a few more questions that I'd like to put to you. I'm wondering whether you have any knowledge, maybe you were even present at the 14th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which took place, I believe, on either the 27th or the 28th of March, 1992, when Mr. Radovan Karadzic appears to have told the delegates who were present that the moment that they arrived home in their municipalities, that they were to urgently establish crisis staffs. I wonder whether you're aware of it or whether you were present and you heard it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Which year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: 1992. It's either the 27th or the 28th of March, 1992, and that was the 14th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. I think it was actually maybe even in your hometown of Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was the 27th, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The 27th. Thank you very much, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. It shows my sources are incorrect. In any event, the Assembly meeting on the 27th of March, 1992, and Mr. Karadzic seems to have told the delegates then, in March 1992, that the moment that they arrive back in their municipalities, that they must urgently establish crisis staffs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, but I do know that Radovan Karadzic, as president of the Republic, was indeed in Samac in 1994. I can't remember which session of the peoples' assembly of Republika Srpska was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether you could take a look at an exhibit which is numbered P124, in the ter version for Mr. Mitrovic, please. You're familiar with this document, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And if you'd turn to -- I only have the English version in front of me, but if you'd turn to the second page of the preamble, it's signed -- or it has the name of a person. Is that yourself, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. Could we have maybe for the benefit of our clients on the ELMO this particular part, and then maybe the witness can turn around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette of the municipality of Samac, year 1, number 1, 3rd June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. So is this your name on page 2 of the preamble?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And it says on the first page of the preamble, amongst other things, in the third paragraph, the last sentence, that: "The Crisis Staff was assigned the task and vested with the authority to exercise the functions of the highest organ of authority of the Serbian municipality and to coordinate cooperation and activities with Serbian Territorial Defence units." Is that correct in terms of what you're reading in the B/C/S version? And my question is simply: Was that the case? Is this correct, what that sentence says, which you appended your name to on the second page?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is the first issue, the first number of the Official Gazette, published when conditions were created to publish it, when there was enough money to publish the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Mitrovic. I understand, yes, in most countries of the world, gazettes or official publications come out sometimes long after the actual meetings they're recording. But my question is specific. If you turn to the preamble, which you have signed, I might maybe ask you directly: Did you actually draft the preamble yourself, as well as append your name to it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did write it, and I took part in the drafting of this preamble. It was proofread and certain details were verified on the basis of interventions made by Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Fine. And that sentence that I read out, which is the last sentence of the third paragraph, concerning the Crisis Staff's task being to exercise the functions of the highest organ of authority, et cetera, that, in your view, having written this, is correct? Am I right in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the final proofreading of this text before it was printed had been done by Dr. Blagoje Simic, which means that he made a number of interventions into the text itself, and this section in particular also. I knew some of the information chronologically here, as it says, certain numbers of the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. But the section that you have pointed out, it has been included on the basis of a proposal and suggestion by Dr. Blagoje Simic, because this text had to be checked by Dr. Blagoje Simic before it was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll leave this particular document, but we might come back to it a little bit later on in a different context. But I would simply ask you, before doing so, just to turn to, in the body of the text itself, the page after the preamble, Article 4, which states: "The highest organ of authority of the Serbian people in terms of the rights and duties of the municipality shall be the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo," et cetera. And then Article 5, if you could maybe just have a read of Article 5 yourself. And I just have one small question.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Does Article 5 mean that only persons of Serbian ethnicity could be members of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision -- excuse me, this is an enactment which I received after it had been drafted already and completed, and that's how it was published, in that very form. And what it says is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And so in response to my question, as a lawyer yourself, your reading, does it mean only persons of Serbian ethnicity, or can it be interpreted in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I can't give you an accurate answer, because I did not take part in the drafting or in the preparation of this decision. But that's how it seems, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And lastly, at least for the moment, I wonder whether, to your knowledge, whether the Crisis Staff, while you were secretary to it - excuse me. I've moved away from this document now, so the usher can maybe sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether, during your term of office as secretary to the Crisis Staff, whether, to your knowledge, the Crisis Staff issued orders, decisions, or conclusions concerning the securing of control of the municipality, securing control of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify? What sort of control exactly are we talking about? I'm not familiar of any specific decision. If I understand you correctly, that is, your question, you're asking me whether the Crisis Staff adopted a decision to place under its control the whole of Bosanski Samac. Is that what you were asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that and also whether the Crisis Staff discussed coordination of civilian administration and military administration to secure Bosanski Samac from perhaps outside forces and perhaps from elements within the municipality itself.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I do not know of any specific decision by the Crisis Staff on control over Bosanski Samac or any order to carry out combat operations by military units. I'm not familiar with anything like that, or at least I can't remember anything like that. But I do believe that a member of the Executive Board - I'm not sure of the Crisis Staff as well - was the chief of the police. Now, whether that implied that he was also a member of the Crisis Staff in this sense or not, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And lastly, and really just following up on that response: Was there a military person, or shall we say a military presence, on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, when a military operation, which I think was named Operation Corridor, was carried out, where military units of Republika Srpska linked up in Modrica, and when the units from Krajina came to the area of Posavina, I believe that a commander of one of those units once came to the Crisis Staff, the commander of a unit which had certain tasks probably in our area. He came to see Dr. Blagoje Simic. I didn't know his name. Was it the 2nd Krajina Brigade, the name of the unit or not, I really can't remember right now. But I thought that this was a ceremonial visit, not really an official visit. I'm not sure whether any specific decision was adopted there in terms of who was in charge of the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll have a few questions a little bit later on, but thank you for those responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mitrovic. I'll take my starting point in the document you have in front of you. It has been tendered into evidence and bears the number P124. And if you turn to page 2, at least in the English version, paragraph 4, it is said that the Crisis Staff was formed in the Sava hall of the church of the Holy Mother in Obudovac on the 15th of April, 1992. In other words, at the same place where you were residing, as you have told us. Were you perhaps present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you have any information of that meeting, that it would take place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. The 15th of April, I remember very clearly. On that day I was on my way to Brcko, because my wife was having a baby in Brcko. So I was on my way to Brcko to pick them up. As far as this information concerning the 15th of April is concerned, I obtained it from Dr. Blagoje, when, in the preamble, as Judge Williams called it, when we published the Official Gazette, that was when Dr. Blagoje mentioned the 15th of April, in reference probably to the imminent threat of war. And yes. Furthermore, these decisions that were published here, this decision on the establishment of an assembly of the Serbian people referred to by Judge Williams, and two or three other enactments, those were enactments or decisions that had been adopted, and I found them in a file when the Official Gazette was being prepared for publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. You already told us that you were appointed secretary of the Samac Municipal Assembly on the 28th of March, 1992, didn't you? That's correct? Yes. But in addition, you performed certain tasks as a secretary within the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those were no official positions or appointments. Those were purely technical activities: Typing, proofreading, harmonising different versions of a text and then sending documents to be signed by Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But a while ago you told us that during the meetings you took notes of what happened during the meeting and then you drafted some kind of text to be sent forward to, as I understood it, first and foremost to Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At those meetings that I attended, no standard minutes were being kept, not the usual way. Most often, at the end of a meeting, I would just take down a number of basic things and features that were discussed and decided. And then after that, these notes would be typed out, or rather, the enactment would be typed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But aren't those tasks -- you performed typical tasks of a secretary? Aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by -- or rather, how you see these duties and activities, but these were the activities, what I've just described. That's what my tasks were. I did not attend all the meetings. I did attend a few of them, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So if I understand you correctly, you were never formally appointed secretary of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe Dr. Simic did order once. I think there was a decision typed out, an enactment, a formal decision appointing me as secretary of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I can't remember the date, not the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit D55/1. I assume that you have seen this document before, because it's signed by you yourself.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are data sent over for salaries to be paid, sent over to the Executive Board. But I am not positive that this document is accurate, because what I see here is a name which I don't remember as a member of the Crisis Staff. I don't remember that this person ever came there or received a salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: In this document you are listed as a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is related to the Crisis Staff, but this is not the composition of the Crisis Staff. These are not its members. These are persons who were present on the premises where the Crisis Staff held its meetings. You see, Dr. Blagoje Simic, Mitar Mitrovic, Savo Popovic, et cetera, these are not all the members of the Crisis Staff. Saja Tesic, Milos Ilic, Jovan Ostojic. I don't know about the rest of them, but I know about my personal name, which is not here because I was a member of the Crisis Staff, and I'm sure Simo can confirm this. That was a generally known fact, namely, that I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: For what reason are you listed here as a member of the Crisis Staff, with your signature?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Right here. Yes, it's my signature, but the signature does not mean that I was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But if you take a look at what is under number 3 -- no. Excuse me. Under number 2, Mitar Mitrovic, and the next column, member. You have signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the authenticity of this document, but one thing I know for sure that is that I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I have no possibility of verifying the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave that. As answer to a question put to you by Presiding Judge Mumba, you gave as an answer to who were the members of the Crisis Staff, you talked about Dr. Nogic from the health centre, director of Uniglas; Begovic, representatives of the post office, the water supply. But according to an answer you gave somewhat later, I understood that these were people coming to the Crisis Staff and not members of the Crisis Staff. But could you be so kind and to the best of your recollection list the members, the real members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. I never said that those people were members of the Crisis Staff. Meetings of the Crisis Staff, the meetings I attended, several meetings, were attended by Mr. Blagoje Simic, I believe Savo Popovic, Simeun Simic, Bozo Ninkovic, I believe Mr. Tadic, and some sessions were also attended by other persons who came every now and then. The composition of the Crisis Staff, I don't know what the permanent line-up, in a manner of speaking, was. Mr. Simic should know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you now. What about the chief of the police, Mr. Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: He came too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Came, but was he a member?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I simply can't tell you, because I did not see a single decision on the appointments to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. During the meetings you attended, there were certainly certain members of the Crisis Staff who were present more frequently than the others. Can you please tell us who those members were most frequently attending, except Dr. Blagoje Simic. I understand he was the president. But the other members, like Miroslav Tadic and Todorovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that those were mostly Tadic, Popovic, Simic, Simeun Simic, Milan Simic, Mirko Lukic also came, Bozo Ninkovic would also be there. If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Zaric came once too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But not in the capacity of a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I'm going to turn away from the membership of the Crisis Staff and ask you about a quite different subject. Are you aware of -- or were you aware of the arrival of Serbian paramilitaries or so-called volunteers in Batkusa around mid-April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you become aware of that? Anybody told you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I learned about that quite a bit later, when I'm not sure whether the indictments had already been published, but I learned a lot later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you have any personal experience of the behaviour of these paramilitaries or volunteers on the 17th of April or thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I heard about arrests being made at the police station, and I remember one event in May or June 1992. In this period, I was mostly staying in Obudovac, and a woman from Obudovac found me. I was at the civilian staff building in Obudovac. Dr. Simic sent me there immediately after late April 1992, but I may come back to this later. Anyway, this lady came to the civilian staff building for protection, in Obudovac, and she complained that her husband had been locked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Samac. By the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Regular police or those coming from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which members of the police. But as I knew the man and the lady - he was a Muslim. His name is Kemal Kohnic - together with the head of this staff for protection in Obudovac - his name is Novak Tanasic - I asked to be received by the chief of police. We went there, the two of us. We explained the reasons for our being there, because we knew the man, and we asked whether there was really any legal basis for his arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Was the behaviour of the volunteers or the paramilitaries, whatever you want, on the 17th of April and thereafter ever reported to the Crisis Staff and discussed at any of its meetings, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of these problems and whether they were discussed at any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff, especially not during the period of May, June, and July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But in April?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, or maybe I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you become aware of an explicit decision by the Crisis Staff to take over the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P71. Do you recall this document? Please read the preamble and the first paragraph of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to read this aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No. Just to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: You don't recall that such a decision was taken by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that, absolutely not; at least, as far as I know, and especially this date here, the 15th of May. During that period, that is, May, June, and July, I was mostly in Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P99. Just cast a glance on it and familiarise yourself with the document. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document either, but I'm familiar with the situation which was to be found in Odzak at that time. I heard about these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: So you didn't draft this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. You said -- you told us earlier that the activities of all the political parties was prohibited in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was the activities of the SDS also prohibited or frozen?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the activities of all the political parties were forbidden, that is, in Republika Srpska, in the Serbian Republic, and that also includes the SDS. And that lasted during a certain period of time in 1992, but I cannot tell you the exact period when that ban was in place. I can't remember the period when that was in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Could document P113, 113, be placed before the witness. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: It is signed by you, yourself.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had the authority to do that by Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Wasn't there a deputy president within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether a deputy was appointed or who that was, but I do remember this document, and I remember that Dr. Simic ordered me to sign it. I believe that he at the time was absent, or was supposed to go somewhere. In any case, he ordered me to forward this urgently to Mr. Todorovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I would like to have Exhibit P83 shown to the witness. As you can see, this is a document or a decision issued by the War Presidency of Samac municipality. Have you seen this document before? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document, and I remember when approximately was the session at which this document was drafted and when a vote was given in favour of appointing this commission. Let me just say to you that I believe I did not attend that particular session, but I received an instruction from that session to type up this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: It's dated on the 2nd of October, 1992, as you can see. Exchanges were carried out before that date. Who were in charge of those earlier exchanges? Can you -- do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember this period of May, June, and July. Once during that period I was in that building where the Crisis Staff had its offices, there was a meeting in progress, and Mr. Tadic was one of the people who attended that meeting. I believe that one of the topics was exchange. I heard that that was one of the issues discussed at that meeting, or the issue discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this document with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Did you discuss the content of this document with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. What do you mean when you say "did you discuss this document"? This was an instruction I received after the meeting for me to type up this document. This means that at the meeting, a decision was made that this commission was appointed, just like it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If you didn't discuss this document with anybody else, did you have any personal reflections about the content of Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. The document was typed as per instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Could document P98 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just intervention, Your Honour. I do apologise. If the document could accordingly be put on the ELMO for the benefit of our client, because we have the instructions that they would like to view such material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: You've never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one final question. If I understood you correctly, you -- based on your notes which you took during the meetings you attended of the Crisis Staff, you took notes, and on the basis of your notes, you drafted the text, the draft text of any decision, order, or conclusion; and then you handed it over to the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Blagoje Simic. My question is the following: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic go through, read through your drafts thoroughly and carefully before he signed it, or perhaps ask for amendments in the text?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic read every enactment that was passed either at the Crisis Staff or at the War Presidency, that is, those enactments that I typed up. I'm talking about those documents that were -- the results of those sessions that I attended. Many enactments were drafted based on the proposals put forward by the Executive Board, because it was the members of the Executive Board who attended the sessions of both the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: And one final short question. Were the drafts you prepared, before they were signed, circulated between the other members of -- or the members of the Crisis Staff before Dr. Blagoje Simic signed the text?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. No further questions. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, just a few other points I'd just like to raise with you. To your knowledge, did the Crisis Staff report to, shall we say, central state organs of Republika Srpska concerning the activities of the Crisis Staff and later the War Presidency in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific case, because obviously I can't talk about the sessions at which there were discussions about the things that would be forwarded to the organs of Republika Srpska. But I do remember that the minister for agriculture came. That was Mr. Nadezdin. And he was together with Mr. Milan Simic, the president of the Executive Board. The topic of their conversation, I don't know. I can only assume what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next: At the meetings of the Crisis Staff that you attended, were police issues or military issues ever discussed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically that the work of the police, at least at the meetings that I attended, was ever discussed. There was an episode or an event, if I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I have just remembered. That there was a second episode involving Mr. Todorovic, this second one that I remember. That was a case when a priest was arrested. I believe he was a priest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. On that note, Mr. Mitrovic, maybe it's, being that you have raised this, it was an issue that I myself was going to ask you a question on. I wonder whether the witness could be shown Exhibit P82, please, in the ter version, and if it could also be put on the ELMO for the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe we should be in private session for this, Your Honours. There's a name in that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's correct. Thank you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Maybe I should therefore just repeat the question. Are you aware, and if you're not, simply say so, of a recommendation by the government of Republika Srpska, in its conclusion of 21st of May, 1992, that crisis staffs be abolished so that the army can take over defence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
