utterances.text: As far as I remember, a decision was adopted by the government of Republika Srpska, or the presidency of Republika Srpska. I'm not sure on that one - a decision envisaging the possibility to appoint War Commissions. The Official Gazette, our copies of the Official Gazette, would arrive a bit late - excuse me - in view of our communication with Pale, because the Official Gazette was published in Pale. And I remember those problems too. We would receive our copies with a certain delay. I know that I went to see Mr. Veljko Kostovic, the manager, or rather, the editor of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Mitrovic. I mean, I understand delays and so on and so forth, but if you could just tell me whether you're aware of this conclusion of May 21st, 1992, that I mention, and if you're not, simply say you're not.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, but the Official Gazette, this particular copy arrived late, in July perhaps. I'm not sure. So yes, I did find out about that, but at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question is: Are you aware of any personal contacts between Dr. Blagoje Simic, in his capacity as president of the Crisis Staff, any personal contacts between himself and General Mladic regarding military operations and command problems?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. I have no such information, no information that General Mladic ever came to Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not necessarily that he came, but any contact. It could be on the telephone or fax or some other means of communication, personal contact in any shape or form. Are you aware?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the members of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac wear uniforms or carry weapons, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, they didn't. But at the beginning of war operations, which means in late April, everyone had been mobilised, and everyone was wearing uniforms. Very soon, however, those who attended sessions of the Crisis Staff, they were not -- they did not attend wearing uniforms or carrying weapons. There were one or two persons there who were providing security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the witness could be shown Exhibit P108. This is the decision on renaming the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. Is it time for a break or shall we continue to work? I don't know what is the -- I do apologise. It's my mistake. I thought it's 5.30. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. So do you have the document in front of you there, Mr. Mitrovic? This is the decision on renaming the town of Bosanski Samac. I'm wondering whether you would be able to tell us who drafted this.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted following a proposal by the Executive Board at the session at which this decision was adopted, and as this was a very important thing, renaming the town of Bosanski Samac, it was an important decision to take. This decision was adopted on the initiative of the Executive Board, I believe, and it was drafted at that session, the wording of the decision. I think both Milan Simic and Mirko Lukic attended this session, as well as the remaining members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Who actually put pen to paper or fingers to typewriters and actually gave hard copy to the discussion and the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This enactment, or rather, its very wording, was drafted, the proposal of the Executive Board, and finally it was typed up following the session during which it was discussed. It was then taken, or rather, brought to the members of those who had attended the session, to read it, to have a look, to insert corrections, if necessary. If I'm not mistaken, I think it was also sent to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature on the bottom right hand?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Simic's signature looks very much like this, as far as I know, this should be his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you, and I just have two final questions. One concerns an issue that you've already addressed in a couple of contexts this afternoon, and that is the relationship between the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac. And what I would like to know, based on your personal knowledge and experience as the secretary of the Crisis Staff and so on: Did the Executive Board report to the Crisis Staff? Did the Crisis Staff decide on issues presented to it by the Executive Board or was the Executive Board autonomous and could make decisions in its own right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a short intervention. What we heard in B/C/S version, that the word "report" is -- word "report" in English was translated in terms of inform, which I don't believe that this sense was in Her Honour Judge Williams'. So maybe if I well understand, maybe we could speak about the subordination or in terms of the constitution, et cetera, and the de jure, de facto issues, because otherwise it might be imprecise issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you Mr. Pantelic. Maybe Mr. Mitrovic has understood your intervention. Maybe I can put it in another way. Was the chairman or chairperson of the Executive Board responsible, or shall we say subordinate to the municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of my testimony today, I said that the Crisis Staff, the way I understood the functioning of the Crisis Staff, replaced in part the authorities of the Municipal Assembly, and by virtue of that, it had a relationship with the Executive Board, the same kind of relationship that the Municipal Assembly before it had. And precisely because of that, and in order to clarify this situation, a decision was adopted, as far as I remember, on the Executive Board. This decision contained a list of duties or tasks to be carried out by the Executive Board. Its relationship to the Municipal Assembly or the War Presidency was also defined. This, after all, was regulated by the then existing law on the state administration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which said this, and this decision on the Executive Board merely repeats this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry. I think just for the sake of clarity, maybe if the witness could just be shown briefly P42, which is the decision on the Executive Board and administrative bodies, and maybe you could have a quick look at it and tell us whether it is the decision which you've been giving us this explanation on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There's a correction here. It's actually P1 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's P112, not Exhibit P42. That's Exhibit P112. So, Mr. Mitrovic, is this the document that you were referring to, the decision that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So it does say in Article 1 that the board, Executive Board shall report to the Assembly. In Article 3, it says that the Crisis Staff shall decide in the selection of the chairman and members, and then as you say Article 7 gives a list of duties. And then I wonder whether you could look at Article 10, and you can see that states that the Crisis Staff shall cancel or annul any decision of the Executive Board. In your view, based on your experience in the Crisis Staff, what would your interpretation of that be, in terms of subordination of the Executive Board to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Article 8 [as interpreted] contains the tasks and duties and authorities of the Executive Board -- Article 7. These are also legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's actually Article 10, though, I think, is the one I'm most interested in.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Executive Board performed its duties. I don't know whether any decisions of the Executive Board were discussed at Crisis Staff meetings, as decisions to be annulled or disputed or cancelled. The Executive Board did not send all its documents to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As a lawyer and a secretary to the Crisis Staff, would Article 10, a fair reading of Article 10, suggest that the Crisis Staff had that capacity, in the right circumstances, to cancel or annul decisions of the Executive Board, not in conformity with the constitution, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the decision says and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one last question. It does, however, refer to four documents, but it's the same question related to all four. So I'll just give the numbers. Perhaps if you could see them all at the same time. They're all very short, just one-page documents. P74, P76, P96, and P97. So that's 74, 76, 96, and 97, all Prosecution exhibits. So, Mr. Mitrovic, you've taken a look at these four documents? So just one question.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And the question is simply this: Did the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac provide, number one, recruits, soldiers, men of military age; number 2, supplies, whether it be food, uniforms, weapons; and 3, any other type of logistical support for military units operating in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as these enactments are concerned, I'm not familiar with these. This is dated May and June. I'm not aware that anything related to the use of military or security was discussed at the Crisis Staff, at least while I was there. But pursuant to the law on defence of Republika Srpska then in force, when there is an imminent threat of war or a state of emergency, the municipal bodies and the Executive Board and the municipality itself have the obligation to get involved and assist in defence. That's what the law says, the law on defence of Republika Srpska, and that's that. Now, as for these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, you have not seen these documents before. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take our break, and since we are a little late, I think we shall continue at about a quarter past, 1815 hours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I thought maybe -- I was following the list of exhibits, so I thought maybe some other questions will arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. We simply listed these exhibits in case we needed to use them all. But otherwise it hasn't become necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Mitrovic. Tell me: Do you know if at the end of 1991/beginning of 1992, was there a Croatian community of Bosanska Posavina created?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know which area this Croatian community covered? I would like to know if within the boundaries of that area was situated the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further, I would like to know if you can tell us: After the plebiscite of the Serbian people in November of 1991, was there a creation of the Peoples Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are facts that are very well known by all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since we all come from the -- both of us, we come from the same legal system, I would like us to try to explain to the Chamber the Peoples Assembly was the actual legislative body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the executive power was within the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within the government, there were various ministries, such as the Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Agriculture, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska, this was published as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The lowest form of the local government was the Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could we have Exhibit P124, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, could you please take page 4. I believe that that is the page that was put before you. For the Trial Chamber and our learned friends, it is a document, it talks about a decision about the creation of Pelagicevo, and I would like us to talk about Article 6 of this decision. Mr. Mitrovic, we know that Serb deputies in the parliament of BH were overpowered in terms of voting by the Croatians and the Muslims. If I tell you that Article 6 of this decision foresees the creation and the functioning of the Municipal Assembly only if the interests of the Serb people are infringed --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if you allow me: In two or three sentences, I would like to explain, if the Trial Chamber allows me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I shall try to explain. A decision that the defendant is talking about, the decision about the creation of municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo was rendered on the 29th of November -- 29th of February, 1992, and it was the deputies of Serb nationality that were present. I did not attend that session. This decision was handed and shown to me. It was already passed. But this decision, if I believe, was adopted when the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a decision regarding the referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time, the Serb deputies were outvoted. And that is the situation in the statute of the Republika Srpska. If, for instance, the Assembly of the Republika Srpska of today was to render a decision that it should be rejoined to Serbia, it would constitute an infringement of vital rights of the Bosnians in Republika Srpska, and it is for sure that such a decision could not be adopted today and could not be passed as a decision. And with regards to this, I consider that even then, this is precisely what happened at the time, the infringement of the rights of one people, and such a decision on behalf of Serb deputies were conditionally adopted. The Article 6 which you are mentioning talks about the fact that Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac is adopting the regulation at the federal level and of Bosnia-Herzegovina if it does not infringe the interests of the Serb population. And because it was an outvoting and the referendum -- the decision about the referendum with regards to the independence, this is exactly what happened. So this is how this article can be interpreted. However, regarding Article 5, when Judge Williams asked me about this, it does say that the Serb deputies make up that Assembly. But Article 6 can perhaps explain why this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like you to go to the next page, page 5. It is a decision about the functioning of municipality of Samac. It says the secretary of the Assembly has to help the president of the Assembly with regards to the organisation and so on and so forth. We talked about this, Professor Nikolic talked to us about the law. But I would like to know what is your personal opinion as a legal person. Could you tell us exactly what this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the transcript is completely clear, perhaps Mr. Pantelic could tell us which article he's referring to, the decision number and the article of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a problem of transcript. I will repeat it. It's Article 8 of the Decision of the Temporary Rules of Municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, just to be clear, in our translation is says, Decision on Provisional Rules of Procedure of the Samac Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have jurists that come from various legal systems, but let's talk about our legal system from which we both come from. Could you please describe to us, Mr. Mitrovic, what is the role that plays the president of the Municipal Assembly? We know in Bosnia right now there is a mayor. It is a function that resembles the one that exists in the west. But at the time we did not have a mayor but we had the president of the Municipal Assembly. What was the role of that person with respect to other deputies? Did that person, the president, have more rights, more rights of votes, et cetera, et cetera? How was that applied in practice?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: If we talk about the president of the Municipal Assembly, as far as I know, and I believe that I can explain this, since even today I deal with these things. Now I have much more experience, I'm more a professional right now. But the president of the Municipal Assembly is the first person amongst equals, and he presides the sessions of the Municipal Assembly. He is a deputy of that same Assembly. He calls the sessions of the Municipal Assembly. He is the one who proposes the points to be discussed, and he is the one who proposes the points of the agenda, the items on the agenda that will be discussed, and he is also the one who raises other enactments, raises discussions about other enactments which are proposed to him by the Executive Board, and all this is then discussed at the Municipal Assembly. The secretary is the person who will help and assist during the preparation of this Assembly, the secretary sends the material to various deputies, convenes the session, and takes care of other technical aspects. Now, today, within the Republika Srpska, we have a mayor, and at the time there was the Executive Board. But it is the same body, the same executive body, which has operative, executory duties, that is the body that is a representative of the policies of the municipality and the president of the Assembly does not have all that many rights, if I may say so. So I'm trying to explain to you what the Municipal Assembly is like and the president of the Assembly, of the Municipal Assembly, what that person would do. And just one more sentence. When the War Presidency stopped or ceased to exist, the Municipal Assembly had its full -- or started working in its full capacity. The president of the Assembly and the secretary were also there, and the procedure was established enabling this body to exist and to function. So the president of the Assembly, if this is what you're thinking of, did not have any more rights than the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During war, and you will certainly agree with me that it is necessary to make decisions in a quick manner, and so the government of Republika Srpska had to adopt decisions and the ministries had to make decrees at the time to issue decrees very quickly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Those decrees stemming from the government were necessary for the ministries to function at the level of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and with regards to the Executive Board as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As a person who has experience in this field, as a lawyer, could you please explain the Trial Chamber who was at the level of the Municipal Assembly, or who at the level of the Municipal Assembly had a greater power in terms of budget, organisation? Was it the Executive Board or was it the Municipal Assembly or if such a body could not convene, was it the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Up until that time -- at the time, actually, I had just graduated. So in 1992 I had some experience, but not that much, with regards to the functioning of municipal bodies. Now I have much more experience, of course. I can say it openly. But the fact is the following: The Executive Board, since this is what you're asking me to explain, had the power to dispose of the budget, so they are the ones who had to deal with the pay, payment of salaries for the people who were working, they could dispose of the money that was going to be spent for everything they needed, and for other outlays.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With regards to a question that was posed to you by the Honourable Judge Williams, you've answered that during the war, in times of war, the local municipality, as a body of the Municipal Assembly, had to help with regards to food and to distribute food and other important staples, and that was its duty, if I do not -- if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, the law of the National Defence stipulated this. This is how it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But the process of recruiting -- and who was recruiting members? Who was filling out the ranks of the military?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This process of recruiting members and deploying those members of the reserve army members, at the time it was the Ministry of Defence, and it went down the ladder, all the way down to the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the specific structure of the police force, that is, the ministry of the exterior [as interpreted] and the army and bearing in mind that subordination, tell me, according to the regulations that were in force at the time, in 1992 and 1993 was the Municipal Assembly in a position to issue orders either to the police or the military? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the use, the combat use of the army units and the police units was not within the purview of any of the municipal organs, even if they had wanted to do so. There was the law on the Ministry of the Interior and the internal affairs which regulated the tasks, duties, and the use of police, and there was also the law on National Defence, which regulated the issues pertaining to mobilisation, the use of army units, Territorial Defence, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit P112, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was about this decision. You provided us with a lot of details. However, in order to clarify things, when we look at Article 7 of this decision, we can see a rather wide spectrum of duties and obligations of the Executive Board. You have talked in great detail about that. Will you agree with me when I say that at the local level, effectively the Municipal Assembly was a legislative body and that the Executive Board had a number of operational functions which are envisaged by Article 7 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: One could say that the Municipal Assembly was some sort of a legislative body and had legislative functions at the local level. Obviously, it could not pass decisions in the form of a law. It could only adopt other more general enactments. As for the authorities and competencies of the Executive Board which are given in Article 7 of this decision, those are also given in the law on state administration which was in force at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now if we look at Article 8, it's paragraph 2, will you agree with me if I say that effectively the Executive Board was in charge of the organisation of the totality of the life in the municipality and that it was duty-bound to inform the Municipal Assembly of -- on its activities and results? In other words, isn't it true that the Executive Board was independent in what it did?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can say that the Executive Board was at that time a body which performed its legal tasks and duties, including the ones that you've mentioned. For that matter, at the few sessions of the Crisis Staff that I attended, and based on the knowledge that I have on that matter, representatives of the crisis -- of the Executive Board --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: -- did come to those meetings. The president of the Executive Board and its vice-president, and others as well, if that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. Let me just look at an enactment that I have here, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P113, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened a long time ago, but I would like to refresh your memory. The last sentence, i.e., the paragraph 2 of this decision, reads: "The presence of the War President, for objective reasons, has been prevented from coming because he was injured and therefore in treatment." Do you remember that at that time Dr. Simic was absent because he had been wounded and had to be treated for that wound? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember, as far as I can, but I know for a fact that he ordered me to type this urgently and hand it over to Todorovic. He was absent indeed, because he had to go for this treatment that you've mentioned. And that is why, at the place of the signature, it says "on behalf of the War Presidency." It doesn't say "the War Presidency or the secretary of the War Presidency or president of the War Presidency." It says "signed on behalf or for the War Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that among the members of the Crisis Staff, there were members of various political parties, that there were members of the reformists, of liberals? We're talking about the year 1992, and that there were also people that did not belong to any of the parties. Are you aware of that? Can you tell us if you are aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I must say that at that time, I didn't know almost anybody among those people who featured as members of the Crisis Staff. I had never met them before. I didn't know them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you get to know them later on?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Later on I also learned that some of them were not members of the SDS or had not been its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: As regards the implementation of certain state regulations at the local level, did these regulations ever come from the SDS as a party, or did they come from the competent organs of the government, for example, ministries?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I must repeat, and I've already said that the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska, during that period of time, that is, in 1992, arrived with a delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you. You've already explained that. Was the SDS the body that adopted regulations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was not the SDS. It was the government Republika Srpska or its competent bodies, ministries and other bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, remember not to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- well, Your Honour, of course that was not my intention, since the witness already explained that in response to the Chamber's question, I just wanted to wind up, since I'm limited with time. But I will of course take care about it. Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have Exhibit P88, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, have you ever seen this decision? Did you maybe participate in its drafting? Can you please put it on the ELMO so that our defendants can also see it. Maybe you can have a look at it first, a closer look at it first, and then return it on the ELMO. But please take your time. I don't want to rush you. Just take your time reading this decision. My question is as follows: Since this decision is in the Latinic script and it was typed on a computer, is that what you used in the Crisis Staff, or did you use a typewriter with a Cyrillic script? What was the situation like at the time? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I do not remember this order. I really don't. But I do know that a government's decision was published and that it read something along these lines. You can check that in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. And it is also a decision regarding the confiscated goods or something like that. As for the typewriter, this is not a typewriter, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself use this type of a typewriter or a computer in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't a computer; it was a mechanical typewriter. At that time we did not have a computer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was that a typewriter with a Cyrillic script or a Latinic script?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was a typewriter with a Latinic script, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, please, Mr. Mitrovic: The decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, were they discussed by the Municipal Assembly which was reconvened for the first time when conditions for the beginning of the work of the Municipal Assembly were in place? Do you remember that? Do you remember if these decisions were ever discussed by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that the Municipal Assembly, at that session which was called in December 1992, established a committee or a commission which was to gather all the decisions passed by the Crisis Staff, to sort them out, to look at them, to analyse them, and to report to the Municipal Assembly at the next session and propose them for the ratification by the Municipal Assembly, and this is exactly what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you have any personal knowledge about the work of Stevan Todorovic at a certain period of time being controlled by the commission of the Ministry of the Interior? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't recall any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about the seat of the Crisis Staff. Immediately upon the outbreak of the conflict, was the seat of the Crisis Staff on the premises of the city heating plant?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the organs of the municipality, that is, both the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board, had its premises in the building of the municipality. That is the first days they spent in that company that mentioned. After that, they moved to the municipal building, but soon after that, I don't know after how much time, due to the war operations, the building of the municipality is very close to the Sava River, and there were war operations from the opposite bank, from the side of Croatia, and there was shooting at Samac and on the municipal building. One building close to the municipal building got a flame, and that is when these two bodies had to move again, and I believe that they moved to the building of the heating plant of the town's heating plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the Executive Board and its services, did they continue to occupy the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly the Executive Board operated from the municipal building, save for some short period of time when there were intense war operations. So the Executive Board was continuously there in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge or do you remember whether Dr. Blagoje Simic ever participated in the appointment of military commanders? Did he have that possibility? Were there such situations in which he would appoint a commander in the territory of Samac municipality? If you know that, can you share that information with us.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any such cases. I don't have any knowledge about such cases. But I remember that Mr. Zaric was appointed by him, that is, proposed by him, for the post -- for a certain post in the Ministry of the Interior. I believe that he did that on behalf of the Crisis Staff and the Executive Board, but I -- as I say, I believe that this is the appointment that did take place, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished with my examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since we have only about three minutes, we'll adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow. Tomorrow our session will be in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of April 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
